persona_summary: I am a senior security engineer who has led crypto-library audits at NCC Group / Cure53 / Trail-of-Bits-class shops. I am not anti-PQ on principle and I support eventual hybrid deployment. But my professional posture — informed by 15+ years of seeing what actually goes wrong when crypto code reaches production — is that the dominant failure mode of new crypto libraries is IMPLEMENTATION-level (timing leaks, RNG misuse, allocator-pattern leakage, fault attacks, memory-disclosure, mis-implemented spec edges, build-target divergence), NOT ALGORITHMIC. The hybrid combiner property — strip-resistance against downgrade and protection against algorithmic compromise of either half — addresses the ALGORITHMIC failure class. It is structurally orthogonal to the IMPLEMENTATION failure class, which is the class I would bet money on hitting first. Production-deploying an unaudited PQ library as the v1-beta DEFAULT (not opt-in, not feature-gated, not non-default-arm) shifts a real audit-discipline cost onto Benten. My role here is to evaluate whether the seven PURSUE-set paths handle that cost honestly, with appropriate disclosure and kill-switch posture, and whether Benten is taking on appropriately-bounded security-response liability for what it ships. Where L2 (PQ-skeptic) brought the SCA-literature axis and the specific GHSA-hcp2-x6j4-29j7 timing-leak fact, my lens brings the systematic-audit-discipline axis: how does Benten know when to PULL the unaudited substrate, what's the maximum-exposure window, and how does standalone publication of crypto-adjacent code (F6 library) extend Benten's security-response liability surface.

per_path.path: F5 — Blog post on benten.computer/blog (load-bearing primary signal)
per_path.rationale:
Sharpest objection from my lens. The blog as currently outlined (§3 of strategy doc) fails the audit-discipline disclosure standard in FIVE specific ways, BEYOND the text-changes L2 already requested. I converge with L2 on the implementation-vs-algorithm distinction and the strip-resistance bullet rewrite — DO NOT REPEAT those here, see L2. My five ADDITIONAL audit-discipline failure modes the current draft hits: (1) NO BOUND ON THE v1-BETA EXPOSURE WINDOW. The blog says 'audit is committed v1-beta deliverable + gates v1-GM' (caveat #3). It does NOT say how long v1-beta is expected to last. From the audit-discipline standpoint, an unaudited PQ library deployed as default for an indefinite window IS the security posture being disclosed; saying nothing about that window IS the disclosure failure. The blog must commit to a maximum target window (e.g. '6 months target, 12 months hard ceiling') OR explicitly disclose 'window duration is open-ended; we will publish quarterly status updates.' The current 'gates v1-GM' framing reads as if v1-GM is imminent — the timeline (Section 6) shows it is NOT scoped, and no audit-vendor / audit-budget / audit-scope commitments are public. (2) NO KILL-SWITCH POSTURE DISCLOSED. The blog should answer: if a new RUSTSEC advisory drops against `ml-dsa` next week disclosing private-key recovery, what does Benten do? Options range from 'immediate emergency point-release pinning around the bug class' through 'public disclosure window + opt-in classical-only downgrade arm activation' to 'rotate-all-keys advisory.' Benten has the crypto-agility framing (CLAUDE.md #5) and the classical-only swap arm is in scope (G-CORE-3c full bidirectional swap matrix per CLAUDE.md baked-in #5) — so the kill-switch capability EXISTS structurally. But the blog needs to disclose it as a posture, not just a capability. Right now the blog implicitly says 'trust us to handle it'; the audit-discipline standard says 'tell us the playbook.' (3) NO SIDE-CHANNEL-OBSERVABILITY POSTURE. ml-dsa's exceptional SCA sensitivity (NIST 2025) means Benten's three deployment shapes (CLAUDE.md #17: native commodity-laptop / browser-wasm32 / Tauri-embedded-webview) have measurably different SCA threat profiles. Browser-wasm32 in particular is the worst case — adjacent-tab attacker JS with sub-microsecond timing observability against a signing path running in a different wasm instance is a known threat regime (cf. Spectre-class browser timing attacks). The blog needs to disclose WHICH shapes are in-scope for the unaudited-substrate risk and what mitigations apply per shape (e.g. is wasm-shape signing using ml-dsa AT ALL during v1-beta, or is signing restricted to native-shape only and wasm-shape uses sealed-sender-style delegation to a native peer?). Without that disclosure the blog implicitly endorses ml-dsa signing in browser context, which is the threat regime where the unaudited substrate is most exposed. (4) NO DEPLOYMENT-CONTEXT EXCLUSION TEXT. L2's persona reached this — 'If you are deploying Benten in a threat regime where local attackers can measure signing timing — e.g. shared-tenancy server hosting signing keys, or a browser tab adjacent to attacker JavaScript — wait for v1-GM.' I reinforce: the blog needs a 'we do NOT recommend Benten v1-beta for [enumerated deployment contexts]' subsection, in plain language, at the top of the safety section. Defining who SHOULD wait is the audit-discipline complement to defining what's shipped. (5) NO INCIDENT-RESPONSE / DISCLOSURE-POLICY POINTER. Standard security-mature project posture: a SECURITY.md / .well-known/security.txt with disclosure window, contact channel, vendor-status update commitment. The blog should link to it. If it does not exist yet, the blog should not ship until it does. This is a prerequisite for shipping crypto-adjacent code as DEFAULT.

If all five additions land (alongside L2's text-changes), my F5 verdict moves to + (full support). If only L2's changes land and these five do not, F5 stays −1 from my lens. If neither lens's changes land, my recommendation is DOWNGRADE to Position A (per L2's downgrade path) AND post the blog as 'Engineering note: how we deploy ml-dsa during the v1-beta audit window' — framing it explicitly as a substrate-discussion artifact not a standards-shaping pitch.

per_path.path: F6 — Open-source did:jwk hybrid extension library (standalone)
per_path.rationale:
Sharpest divergence from L2 here. L2 reads F6 as the BEST single move (asymmetric trust-builder; let community help find issues). I read F6 as a SECURITY-LIABILITY EXPANSION that needs explicit scope-bounding before it lands. Reasoning from audit-discipline:

(a) Publishing a standalone crypto-adjacent library on crates.io + npm under the Benten brand EXTENDS Benten's security-response liability surface beyond the Benten engine itself. Any downstream project that depends on the library and gets bitten by a bug (in Benten's combiner glue, OR in the underlying ml-dsa dependency Benten chose to surface, OR in JWK parsing edge cases the library handles) will (rightly) consider Benten a responsible party in the disclosure + patching + advisory-publishing process. This is real ongoing work. Benten is a small team (per L5 small-team-overreach lens persona) with a v1-beta cliff face of its own to ship. Taking on standalone-crypto-library maintainership liability ON TOP OF the engine-shipping work is a real cost the strategy doc does not budget.

(b) The library's value-prop ('we shipped the code, here it is to inspect') is real but FUNCTIONALLY EQUIVALENT to publishing the relevant Benten engine subtrees under an explicit 'this is the crypto-glue, audit it here' README pointer + a security-reviewer-friendly module layout. The standalone-library packaging adds a publication-and-versioning-and-API-surface contract that is heavier than the actual review-enablement use case requires. A `docs/security/crypto-glue.md` walking through the combiner code in `benten-crypto-suite` (with permalinks pinned to a specific commit) gives reviewers the same scrutiny target with strictly less liability surface.

(c) The strategy doc Section 5 failure-mode D acknowledges this ('reputation-HIGH cost if Benten-authored combiner code; keep library minimal') but the mitigation is one sentence and is not a process. From audit-discipline: 'minimal' is a goal not a contract. The library scope needs an explicit CONTRACT — what's in, what's out, what API surface is stable, what's the response SLA for issues, who's the responsible-disclosure contact, what's the maintenance commitment if Benten the company de-prioritizes the library (does it become orphaned? archived? transferred?). Without that contract published WITH the library, F6 is shipping a security artifact without a security process.

(d) L2 explicitly noted F6 should ship 'test vectors + known-answer-tests against the LAMPS draft-19 spec' — I support that and ADD: the library should commit to a SPEC-DIVERGENCE-TRACKING posture (what happens to the library when LAMPS draft-19 becomes draft-20? draft-25? RFC? The early-allocation of OID `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48` is for the OID NOT the construction — L9's point — and the construction MAY change in WG review). The library needs to publicly commit to either (i) tracking the latest LAMPS draft and bumping the major version on each construction change, OR (ii) freezing at a specific draft and explicitly NOT tracking further changes. Either is fine; ambiguity is not.

Recommendation: DOWNGRADE F6 from 'standalone library' to 'commented + review-friendly Benten engine subtree + docs/security/crypto-glue.md pointer + a security.md disclosure policy applicable to the engine repo as a whole.' If Ben explicitly accepts the standalone-library security-response liability — i.e. budgets the ongoing maintenance + the response-on-disclosure cost + designates an owner + commits to a published response SLA + ratifies the spec-divergence-tracking posture — then F6 becomes acceptable and my verdict moves to NEUTRAL. WITHOUT that explicit acceptance F6 ships a hidden liability that bites when the next ml-dsa advisory drops. The L2 'trust-builder' framing is correct in isolation but does not account for the maintenance-and-response cost on a small team.

The cross-cutting audit-discipline failure mode the strategy doc has NOT yet engaged is the v1-beta-window-bounding + kill-switch-posture + security-liability-budget question: Benten is shipping an unaudited PQ library AS DEFAULT for an unbounded window, taking on standalone-crypto-library publication liability, and lacks a published incident-response posture. None of these are insurmountable — all three are answerable in a few weeks of orchestrator-direct work. objection_1.statement: Isn't the v1-beta-to-v1-GM gate already the answer to your window-bounding objection?
objection_1.response: No — the gate is structural (v1-GM doesn't ship until audit lands) but the WINDOW is unbounded because v1-beta is open-ended. From the disclosure standpoint, 'we will ship v1-GM when the audit lands and we haven't named the audit vendor or budget' is structurally equivalent to 'open-ended.' The gate is necessary but not sufficient. What's needed is either (a) a target date for v1-GM with a quarterly status-update commitment if it slips, OR (b) explicit disclosure that v1-beta duration is open-ended with a published review cadence. Either is honest; saying nothing about the window is the disclosure failure.

objection_2.statement: The kill-switch posture you want is operationally heavy; we're a small team and 72h SLAs are expensive.
objection_2.response: Partly conceded. The SLA numbers in my proposed caveat #7 (24h emergency / 72h advisory) are aggressive and were drafted with a security-mature OSS project in mind. For Benten's actual team size, less aggressive numbers (72h emergency-acknowledgement / 7d advisory / 30d patch-or-mitigation) are defensible — the requirement from my lens is that SOME numbers are published, not specifically my numbers. A small team with 72h/7d/30d SLAs has a more credible posture than a large team with 24h/72h SLAs that go unmet. The discipline-cost is the act of publishing AND meeting whatever numbers are committed. If even 7d/30d is over budget, that's a strong signal F6 (standalone library) should not ship at all — because library publication implicitly creates a 'somebody should respond' expectation, and ignoring it is worse than not publishing the library.

objection_3.statement: Your F6 NEUTRAL-LEANING-NEGATIVE verdict conflicts with L2's STRONG-POSITIVE verdict. Doesn't that mean one of you is wrong?
objection_3.response: No — we are looking at different cost surfaces. L2 weighs F6's TRUST-BUILDING value (high) against the SUBSTRATE-AUDIT-EXPOSURE cost (which L2 considers already-paid by F5's engine-deployment, so library publication adds little marginal cost). My lens weighs F6's MAINTENANCE-AND-RESPONSE liability (which is a NEW cost surface library-publication creates that engine-shipping does not) against the trust-building value. Both readings are internally consistent. The synthesis from Ben's standpoint: L2's trust-building value is real, AND my maintenance-liability cost is real, AND the right call depends on whether Benten can budget the ongoing library-maintenance work — which is a small-team-capacity question Ben is best-positioned to answer. If Ben can budget it, do F6 as L2 recommends with my scope contract attached. If Ben can't budget it, downgrade F6 to engine-subtree pointer per my recommendation. Either decision is defensible; the failure mode is shipping the library without making the budget call deliberately.

objection_4.statement: Your deployment-shape SCA caveat (#8) implies browser-shape signing is currently broken in v1-beta. Is it?
objection_4.response: Truthfully I do not know from the persona's read of the strategy doc + CLAUDE.md alone. CLAUDE.md baked-in #17 says browser-shape is thin-compute and writes go via fetch to a full peer — which would imply signing happens at the full-peer side and browser-shape never invokes ml-dsa signing locally. If that's how it's actually implemented, my caveat #8 just documents the existing architecture and is cheap to write. If the implementation has drifted (e.g. browser-shape has a local signing path for some optimization), then caveat #8 surfaces a bug the orchestrator needs to fix before v1-beta tag. EITHER way the caveat is cheap to ship and the verification work it triggers is something a v1-beta-readiness audit should be doing anyway. If verification confirms browser-shape never signs locally, the caveat reads as a strong design-decision disclosure; if verification surfaces a bug, the caveat triggered a real fix. Win/win.

objection_5.statement: The 'industry baseline disclosure standard' addition (caveat #8d) reads as Benten trying to invent a new standard rather than ship its product. Isn't that scope creep?
objection_5.response: Partly conceded — the wording can be tightened. The substantive point is not 'Benten will author a disclosure standard' but rather 'the absence of an industry-wide pattern is itself a gap that adopters should consider when reading Benten\'s and other adopters\' substrate-disclosure language.' That observation is in scope for a blog discussing PQ-hybrid deployment because it directly bears on what readers should treat as adequate disclosure from any adopter. Reword as: 'We\'d like to see ecosystem convergence on what adequate substrate-disclosure looks like for projects shipping unaudited PQ defaults — the current variance across adopters makes substrate-risk comparison hard for downstream users.' That's narrower and stays within the blog\'s scope.

the_systematic_audit_discipline_question.framing: Beyond the specific F5 + F6 verdicts, the SYSTEMATIC question my lens raises is: does Benten have an organizational SECURITY-OPERATIONS posture appropriate to shipping crypto-substrate code as default? This is a question above the strategy doc's scope but it bears on whether the strategy doc's chosen paths are appropriately-scoped to Benten's actual capacity.
components: (a) Published security policy — security.md / .well-known/security.txt — naming disclosure contact, expected acknowledgement window, expected patch window. Industry baseline: any project with `crypto` in its tagline. Benten\'s current state: unknown to my persona; checkable.

(b) Named security-response owner — single human accountable for incident response. Industry baseline: small projects have one named owner; large projects have a rotation. Benten\'s current state: probably Ben himself; should be named publicly.

(c) Dependency-advisory subscription — automated RUSTSEC / npm-audit / cargo-audit watching of the crypto dependency tree, with on-call notification. Industry baseline: any project shipping crypto-adjacent code has this. Benten\'s current state: cargo-deny is wired in CI per recent dispatch-conventions context; check whether security-advisory feeds trigger orchestrator notification.

(d) Embargo + coordinated-disclosure process — written process for receiving a private disclosure, embargoing it, coordinating patches across affected versions, releasing with advisory. Industry baseline: emerging in security-mature OSS; missing in most small projects. Benten\'s current state: unlikely to exist yet given pre-v1-beta posture.

(e) Spec-divergence tracking — for crypto-adjacent code dependent on a draft spec (LAMPS draft-19), documented process for tracking spec updates and bumping library versions. Industry baseline: rare; what makes it rare is exactly why standalone-crypto-library publication is harder than it looks. Benten\'s current state: not yet established.
the_systematic_audit_discipline_question.lens_recommendation: Before F5 + F6 publish, Ben should explicitly ratify (or defer-with-named-destination per HARD RULE 12) each of (a)-(e). The audit-discipline minimum-viable shape is (a) + (b) + (c) shipped; (d) + (e) committed-with-target-date. Anything less and F5 + F6 ship as security-adjacent artifacts without security-process backing them, which is the structural disclosure failure that bites at the next ml-dsa advisory. If Ben judges (a)-(e) too heavy for the v1-beta window, my STRONG recommendation is to DOWNGRADE F6 to engine-subtree pointer (per my F6 verdict) and DOWNGRADE F5 to Position A (per L2 + my F5 verdict), which together reduce the security-process burden to roughly what Benten\'s pre-v1-beta posture already supports.

what_would_change_my_verdict: If F5 ships with L2's text changes AND my five additional caveats (#3-extension, #7 kill-switch, #8 deployment-shape SCA, #9 deployment-context exclusions, #8d ecosystem-disclosure-standard call) AND a v1-beta-window-target commitment, my F5 verdict moves from −1 to + (full support).

If F5 is downgraded to Position A (per L2's downgrade path), my F5 verdict moves to + without requiring the additional caveats (Position A doesn't make the ecosystem-prescriptive claim that requires the safety-story to be airtight at this depth).

If F6 ships standalone-library AND Ben explicitly ratifies the security-liability scope contract — named maintenance owner, published response SLA, spec-divergence-tracking commitment, security.md published, audit-vendor commitment — my F6 verdict moves from NEUTRAL-LEANING-NEGATIVE to + (full support).

If F6 is downgraded to engine-subtree pointer + crypto-glue docs + security.md (no standalone-library publication), my F6 verdict moves to + immediately (this is the lower-cost path that captures most of L2's trust-building value at strictly less liability surface).

If Benten publishes a security.md before F5 + F6 publish AND establishes RUSTSEC-feed monitoring on the crypto dependency tree AND names a single security-response owner publicly, all six remaining paths' verdicts strengthen by one increment (NEUTRAL→+; + → STRONG-+).

If between now and F5 publish the RustCrypto `ml-dsa` crate receives an independent audit (per Project Eleven's published intent to seek funding), most of my objections evaporate — my F5 verdict would move to + without any text changes required.
